title: Local-moment magnets on all close-packed lattices are equivalent
authors: Sam Studdy, Alwyn Jose Raja, R. Ganesh
abstract: The Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the fcc lattice is a canonical example of frustration. The fcc lattice is but one of an infinite number of close-packed structures, all of which have the same frustration-inducing local geometry. In this letter, we demonstrate a hidden symmetry that relates classical magnets on all close-packed lattices. This symmetry derives from a similar property in tight binding models that may explain the disordered low-temperature structures of lithium and sodium metals. In magnets, the symmetry holds when couplings are restricted to nearest ($J_1$) and next-nearest neighbours ($J_2$). It guarantees that all close-packed lattices are equivalent at the Luttinger-Tisza level. For any given values of $J_1$ and $J_2$, they have the same ground-state energy. Their ground state momenta are identical when projected onto the stacking plane. We construct a unified phase diagram as a function of $J_1$ and $J_2$ couplings for Heisenberg, XY and Ising magnets on any close-packed lattice. In each phase, the ground-state degeneracy is the same on all close-packed lattices, even after accounting for multi-Q spirals. This phase diagram can be easily adapted to any magnet composed of stacked triangular layers with similar couplings. Fluctuations above the classical ground state(s) are not related by any symmetry. This suggests that close-packed structures can show interesting differences in order-by-disorder selection.
summary: This work demonstrates a hidden symmetry proving that the classical ground state energy and degeneracy are identical for local-moment magnets on all close-packed lattices. However, the authors show that while the classical physics is equivalent, quantum fluctuations, such as zero-point energy, are structure-dependent, suggesting that the true low-temperature order can distinguish between these seemingly equivalent lattices.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether local-moment magnets on different close-packed lattices are physically equivalent regarding their classical ground state.
main_result: The classical ground state energy and degeneracy are identical across all close-packed lattices, but fluctuations (zero-point energy and free energy) are structure-dependent, indicating a breakdown of symmetry beyond the classical limit.
method: The analysis uses the Luttinger-Tisza approach to determine classical ground states and compares the resulting energy landscapes and degeneracy spaces across different lattice geometries.
model_or_system: The system is a local-moment magnet described by a Heisenberg antiferromagnet Hamiltonian restricted to nearest ($J_1$) and next-nearest ($J_2$) neighbor couplings on any close-packed lattice (e.g., fcc, hcp).
key_observables: Ground state energy ($E_{g.s.}$), ground state degeneracy, zero-point energy ($O(S)$ correction), and free energy minimum.
important_parameters: Coupling ratios ($J_1/J_2$), lattice geometry (fcc, hcp, etc.), and the spin magnitude $S$.
main_assumptions: The equivalence is proven for the classical limit (Heisenberg model) and extends to XY and Ising models, but fluctuations are not related by the symmetry.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of close-packing, construct a unified phase diagram based on $J_1$ and $J_2$, and compare the location of LT minima and the calculated zero-point energy across different structures.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the hidden symmetry relating classical ground states via the Luttinger-Tisza method, constructing a unified phase diagram. It then analyzes the degeneracy and structure of the ground states in different phases, concluding by contrasting the robust classical equivalence with the structure-dependent nature of quantum fluctuations.
why_interesting: The finding that classical symmetries break down when considering quantum fluctuations (zero-point energy) is a key concept in understanding order-by-disorder selection in frustrated quantum magnets, which is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum magnetism.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. a) A close-packed structure viewed along the stacking axis. Generically, the unit cell forms a rhombus, with primi- tive translations ˆa and ˆb as shown. b) As an example, the unit cell of the ABAC structure is shown. The primitive transla- tion vector ˆc is parallel to the stacking axis. c) The Brillouin zone of an M-layer structure forms a hexagonal prism or (d) a hexagon when projected onto the stacking plane. Momenta of interest are labeled.

FIG. 2. Unified phase diagram for the J1 −J2 model on any close-packed lattice. Phases are labeled by the location(s) of LT minimum (or minima) within the projected Brillouin zone. The table shows the classical ground state energy, Eg.s., on a per-spin basis with the spin length S set to unity.

FIG. 3. a) Two adjacent layers in a close-packed structure. b) Four sublattices spanned by J2 bonds. The four-sublattice structure persists for any number of layers. c) A single-Q ground state in the M phase. Spin orientations are shown in two layers. In subsequent layers, spins are fixed such that each J2-sublattice is ferromagnetically ordered. A single-Q ground state in the (Γ, M) phase is similar, with each J2-sublattice ordered antiferromagnetically. d) A single-Q ground state in the W phase. Spins in other layers are oriented to satisfy the tetrahedron rule – see text.

FIG. 4. Multi-Q ground states. a) A generic ground state in the X phase with a four-site motif in one layer. Spins in other layers are fixed such that each J2 sublattice is ferromagneti- cally ordered. b) A generic ground state in the W phase, with a sixteen-site motif within a layer. Spins in other layers are fixed by the tetrahedron rule.

FIG. 6. Extensive degeneracy in the purely-J1 antiferromag- net at θ = 0◦. To construct a ground state, we start with a layer. Each line of this layer orders antiferromagnetically, with an independent N´eel vector. On the next layer, we choose lines that run in the same direction and order them antiferromagnetically. N´eel vectors are chosen such that each spin is anti-aligned with one spin of the previous layer. This construction can be extended to any number of layers with any stacking sequence. The degeneracy amounts to choosing an independent N´eel vector for each line within any one layer.
